BCG’s analysis of roughly 100 cities over four decades finds that startup ecosystems do not mature simply by accumulating incubators, funds, and research parks. Cities scale twice as fast when they build these ingredients in sequence, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of innovation, customers, capital, exits, and reinvestment.

Innovation and talent must come before investmentA doubling of patent activity was followed by 17.5% more early-stage venture investment, showing that investors respond to commercially promising ideas rather than creating them from scratch.

Corporate customers turn promising startups into investable businessesEstablished companies validate demand and help startups refine their offerings. Singapore’s Trax won Coca-Cola after corporate pilots, ultimately raising more than $1 billion and becoming a unicorn.

Capital matters most after companies have proven they can sellLate-stage funding enables expansion, but only once research and customer demand are in place. Shanghai’s late-stage investment rose from $372 million to $21.2 billion as its ecosystem matured.

Large exits make the system self-sustaining through recyclingExits return money, experienced founders, and operators to new ventures; doubling exits brought 31% more late-stage capital the following year. Policy should therefore remove each next constraint, not endlessly fund early-stage programs.

Over the past two decades, cities around the world have spent billions of dollars trying to become the next Silicon Valley. They have funded research parks, seeded venture funds, and opened incubators—but many have little to show for the money. Our analysis of roughly 100 cities tracked over four decades suggests why. The ingredients that make up a startup ecosystem matter, but what really accelerates growth is implementing them in the right order. The cities that we’ve studied have identified a replicable pattern enabling them to scale their startup ecosystems twice as fast as cities with legacy setups.In our article “Entrepreneurial Capitalism Will Be Built City by City,” we identified five elements shared by successful startup ecosystems: intellectual property (IP) and talent, access to customers, early- and late-stage capital, supportive policy, and entrepreneurial community and culture. Our new research reveals the sequence in which these components work together to generate and sustain growth:IP and talent provide the ideas and the people needed to create promising businesses.Corporate customers confirm demand and create momentum for those businesses.Early- and late-stage capital scales, allowing startups to form and expand.Startup formation accelerates and begins to produce exits.Startups scale into larger exits as capital and the ecosystem grow.Capital and founders from those exits fund and advise the next generation of companies, a process that we call recycling.Policy and culture, the last two ingredients, act as enablers that influence how well the whole process runs. We call this sequence the Entrepreneurial Prosperity Cycle (EPC). (See Exhibit 1.) We tested the links in the cycle in both directions across the top 100 global startup ecosystems and found that they run one way. More patents brought more early-stage investment in the years that followed, more new companies brought more exits, and more exits brought more capital. On the other hand, capital did not bring patents, and exits did not bring new companies.

We treat $10 billion in capital raised in late-stage venture rounds as a benchmark of maturity, reflecting the level of investment needed to develop companies capable of substantial growth and successful exits. São Paulo reached that level 16 years after its first sizable venture investment year, while Singapore reached it in 17 years. Silicon Valley took 21 years, and Boston roughly 32. (See the sidebar, “How We Identified the Fastest-Maturing Cities.”) In cities that reached the benchmark, GDP grew by 12.1% in the following five years, compared to 9.1% for the rest.

In cities that reached the benchmark, GDP grew by 12.1% in the following five years, compared to 9.1% for the rest.

How We Identified the Fastest-Maturing Cities

An ecosystem reaches self-sustaining momentum when its exits begin to refill it. In our data, that point arrives when the total capital that a city’s companies have raised in late-stage venture rounds passes $10 billion. Beyond that point, exits nearly double, and the money and founders they return are enough to fund the next generation of companies without heavy outside investment.PitchBook, our source, records the total raised in each round, and late-stage rounds often include support from private equity firms, corporations, and sovereign wealth funds investing alongside venture capital firms. The $10 billion therefore counts all capital raised in late-stage venture rounds rather than venture capital alone. The same data let us test how the stages of the cycle affect one another. For each pair—patents and early-stage investment, new companies and exits, and exits and later investment—we asked whether a rise in the first was followed by a rise in the second from one to ten years later, and whether the reverse was also true. Our tests covered 45 to 102 cities, depending on the measure.We measured speed from the year a city first attracted $20 million of venture investment to the year it passed the $10 billion threshold. Among the cities that have reached that milestone, those in the fastest quartile took 19 years or less, 16.5 on average, against an average of 28.8 years for the slowest. (See the exhibit.) These are the fastest-maturing cities. They include nine of the 30 highest-ranked cities in StartupBlink’s annual ranking of the world’s startup ecosystems, with São Paulo and Singapore among them. Also on StartupBlink’s list are 14 cities (on four continents) that fall outside the top 30: Vilnius, in 12 years; Kyiv and Hong Kong, in 16; Nanjing, Chennai, Guangzhou, Hyderabad, Dublin, and Denver, in 17; Copenhagen and Melbourne, in 18; and Bangkok, Hamburg, and Barcelona, in 19. With one exception, Jakarta, every city that we have cited as an example in this article is among them.

Most of the cities that have cleared the $10 billion bar quickly are in wealthy economies, where research universities, deep capital markets, and multinationals were already in place. But some developing cities are catching up, and building in the right order is helping them close the distance. Jakarta ranks 30th among global ecosystems and attracted its first $20 million of venture investment in 2011. The Bandung Institute of Technology opened a Jakarta campus focused on business leadership in 2007. Corporations began opening local offices around 2013 and 2014, and venture investment expanded from about 2017. By 2024, the city’s companies had raised $9.8 billion in late-stage rounds, putting it on the threshold of $10 billion.

These findings challenge the idea that great startup ecosystems are products of exceptional circumstances. The benefits extend well beyond the people who start companies, to the families whose livelihoods depend on the jobs that those companies create and the businesses that serve them. As entrepreneurship becomes self-sustaining, the benefits also reach public budgets, where they may go to schools, housing, and transit improvements that make a city a place where people want to build their lives. It yields prosperity for people who will never found a company.

Build What Investors Need First
In the fastest-maturing cities, venture capital arrived only after their startup ecosystems had built their IP and talent and secured corporate customers. (See Exhibit 2.) Each piece gave the next one something to work with.

Step 1. IP and Talent Create Promising Businesses
Ecosystems need to provide something for capital to latch onto, and that something is commercially promising innovation.Our research found that when an ecosystem increases its production of patented inventions, investment in young companies tends to rise substantially in the years that follow. Across 96 cities, a doubling of patent intensity in one year was associated with 17.5% higher early-stage venture capital investment the following year. The relationship remained positive five years later and was evident in 94% of the cities we studied. Investment did not predict patents in the same way. Its link to later patent activity grew stronger as the lag grew longer, which is a sign of a shared trend, since the effect of a cause fades with time. (See Exhibit 3.)

Across 96 cities, a doubling of patent intensity in one year was associated with 17.5% higher early-stage venture capital investment the following year.

The priority for ecosystems, then, is to develop an expanding base of innovation and the talent to turn it into businesses. That means investing in research, attracting skilled people, and helping entrepreneurs commercialize their ideas. Cities where more than 35% of the workforce has a college degree formed new firms at 1.7 times the rate of cities where that share was below 20%. Dublin built the research and recruited the people for its ecosystem within a generation.

Cities where more than 35% of the workforce has a college degree formed new firms at 1.7 times the rate of cities where that share was below 20%.

In 2000, Dublin’s economy depended on foreign investment, and the government recognized that rising costs would eventually erode that advantage. Its answer was Science Foundation Ireland, which committed €646 million to recruit researchers and build new biotech and IT laboratories. Over the next fifteen years, the city’s research output and patent activity grew, led by Trinity College Dublin and University College Dublin (UCD).To turn that research into businesses, Trinity and UCD partnered with the venture firm Atlantic Bridge on two university spinout funds—Ireland’s first—worth €140 million between them. The funds have backed more than 40 companies, and two of the universities’ spinouts, Inflazome and SilverCloud, have been sold for sums in the hundreds of millions of euros. Trinity now produces the third-most venture-backed founders among universities in Europe, and 310 companies founded by its undergraduate alumni have raised $8.2 billion, according to PitchBook.Step 2. Corporate Customers Confirm Demand
Promising startups need to prove that their business has a market. That means finding customers, often through connections with larger companies. Trax, founded in Singapore in 2010, shows what an established customer can do for a young business. Trax’s founders had originally planned to produce a consumer app, but after meeting with an innovation executive at Procter & Gamble, which ran its Asia-Pacific business from Singapore, they changed their minds. The P&G executive realized that the startup’s underlying technology could solve a problem that large consumer goods companies had struggled with for years, tracking what was on store shelves, and knew that the market for that capability was far larger than the one the founders had in mind. They took the executive’s advice. Two years of pilots with large manufacturers followed, and in 2013 Trax signed its first contract, with Coca-Cola, shortly after raising its first institutional round. The company went on to count Coca-Cola, Nestlé, and P&G among its clients, raised more than $1 billion, and became Singapore’s second unicorn.The kind of encounter that changed Trax’s prospects can be difficult for young businesses to arrange. Hong Kong built a system to make such introductions routine. Cyberport, a government-established technology park housing more than 2,000 companies, matches startups with corporations looking for new suppliers. A corporation identifies a problem, Cyberport shortlists startups that could solve it, and the startups pitch. The network arranges about 100 such sessions a year. Partnerships have included insurer AXA’s adoption of Hex Trust’s digital-asset custody service and Hang Seng Indexes’ use of Wizpresso’s language-processing software.Cities and regions have a vested interest in making these connections easier. All of the fastest-maturing cities in our research developed substantial corporate customer bases before venture investment expanded. Singapore set out in the 1990s to attract regional headquarters, and by 2010, 44% of multinationals with an Asia-Pacific headquarters had located there. From 2009 to 2014, the number of companies with more than $2 billion in revenue grew by 13% a year in Shenzhen and 16% in Singapore. Late-stage venture investment expanded in the ensuing years.Step 3: Early- and Late-Stage Capital Scales
Startups need two kinds of capital. Early-stage money helps companies form. Late-stage rounds, with larger checks and different kinds of financing, let those that have proven their market develop products, enter new markets, and expand. That second kind of capital is what we focus on in measuring a city’s maturity by the capital raised in late-stage rounds, and it is what grew in the fastest-maturing cities once research and customers were in place.In Shanghai, for example, the Focus on Zhangjiang program expanded the city’s universities and research institutes from 1999. Then multinationals set up operations around the Yangshan deepwater port, which opened in 2005, and in the free trade zone that followed it. Venture capital arrived in meaningful amounts in the early 2000s. Late-stage investment rose from $372 million in 2013 to $21.2 billion in 2021, and the city passed the $10 billion threshold in 2015.As more businesses reach the expansion stage, the supply of investment has to grow with them. For cities outside established venture capital hubs, attracting the necessary investment can be difficult. Investors tend to cluster where they have networks, specialist knowledge, and experience backing successful companies. Until a city becomes a venture hub in its own right, it may need to help fill the resulting financing shortages, but the missing capital differs from place to place. Some have few investors willing to back unproven companies; others have enough early-stage funding but lack the larger investments needed to help successful businesses scale.Take Vilnius. Before 2017, the city had almost no local sources of early-stage funding. To attract private investment, Lithuania launched two initiatives. Coinvest Capital, a fund backed by the Lithuanian state and the EU, invests directly in individual startups alongside private investors and gives its co-investors an outsized share of the profits to make participating worthwhile. Meanwhile, INVEGA, a broader state agency, works through lenders and investors, guaranteeing bank loans to early-stage companies and running its own co-investment programs. From 2018 to 2023, the combined value of Lithuanian startups, most of them based in Vilnius, grew 7.1 times, nearly twice the regional average.Lithuania rose to second place in Central and Eastern Europe in venture investment per capita. As more companies secured early funding, later-stage investors gained a larger pool of businesses to back. By 2023, companies in Vilnius had raised $10.5 billion in late-stage financing, including venture capital, private equity, and corporate investment, up from $1.3 billion in 2017. Vilnius reached the $10 billion mark just 12 years after reaching our $20 million threshold, faster than any other city in our research.Hamburg faced a different constraint. A fund established in 2011 had helped launch more than 50 early-stage ventures, but companies that were ready to scale lacked a regional investor that could provide larger investments. In 2024, Hamburg combined €21 million in state funding with €48 million in federal support that established the InnoVentureFonds and its twin program, HamburgInnoGrowth. These €69 million twin funds co-invest with commercial venture firms, providing up to €7 million per company, so that scale-ups can expand globally without leaving the city.Make the EPC Self-Reinforcing
Once ecosystems have developed a strong base of IP, customers, and capital, the next challenge is to make entrepreneurial growth self-sustaining. Accomplishing that task requires a continuing supply of new businesses and the ability to turn the success of established businesses into resources for the next generation. Our data shows how the cycle feeds itself. New companies bring more capital to an ecosystem only through the exits that they produce.Step 4: Startup Formation Accelerates and Begins to Produce Exits
The more startups an ecosystem develops, the more exits it produces. Those exits occur in two main waves: the first within a few years of a company’s founding, and the second after seven to ten years. (See Exhibit 4.) Across 45 cities, we found that a doubling of startup formation was associated with about a third more exits the following year and nearly half again as many ten years on. Exits did not predict formation; the reverse test showed no relationship at any lag.

An ecosystem can stall when formation comes in a single wave. In this scenario, an incubator program or a funding push produces a cohort of companies, a few of them exit early, and the numbers look healthy for several years. But if fewer new companies form behind the first cohort, the pipeline of companies that could reach a large exit weakens—and by the time the slowdown shows up in exits, the city has lost years that it cannot recover.Melbourne illustrates how a mature ecosystem can sustain the formation of new companies. By 2014, the city had passed $10 billion raised in late-stage venture financing, just 18 years after reaching the $20 million threshold, and had produced six unicorns. In 2016, the Victorian government established LaunchVic to help channel the capital and experience generated by successful startups into the next generation of businesses.Over the following years, Melbourne produced another 15 unicorns. Its startup count more than doubled over the decade to 2022, from 1,289 to 3,061, while startup employment grew by 220%, to nearly 28,000 jobs. Successful companies helped finance the next generation, too. After Oracle acquired Aconex, a Melbourne-based construction software company, Aconex’s founders invested some of their proceeds in local startups and venture funds. The acquisition of Melbourne-based payments company Afterpay by Block similarly created a new pool of potential investors, with some former employees becoming angel investors.Step 5: Startups Scale into Larger Exits
The fastest-maturing cities in our research produced exits roughly twice the size of the slowest, a median of $139 million versus $75 million, while the number of exits a year was much the same across every city that reached the threshold. (See Exhibit 5.) Exit size separates faster cities from slower ones because a large exit returns far more to the ecosystem. A sale or listing worth several hundred million dollars generates enough capital to reward founders and fund the startups that follow, and it produces experienced investors and operators to back and run them.

For emerging startup ecosystems, the challenge is to help promising companies sustain their growth long enough to achieve large exits. That means understanding where those businesses stall as they mature and which obstacles cities can help remove. It also means ensuring that, when companies are ready for a major sale or public listing, the region’s financial and regulatory infrastructure can support it.Jakarta shows how consequential that last step can be. By 2020, the city had produced some of Southeast Asia’s largest technology companies, including Gojek in ride hailing and payments, Tokopedia and Bukalapak in e-commerce, and Traveloka in travel services. But its stock exchange was poorly suited to listing them. Founders had no mechanism to retain control through shares with greater voting rights, and listing requirements favored companies with a history of profitability. As a result, some of Jakarta’s most successful startups were considering listings in New York or Singapore.Indonesia responded by revising its capital-market rules. Bukalapak listed in Jakarta in August 2021 and raised $1.5 billion in the largest public offering in the exchange’s history. That December, the financial regulator introduced multiple-voting-share rules to help founders retain control, and the exchange amended its listing requirements to accommodate fast-growing companies. In April 2022, GoTo, formed by the merger of Gojek and Tokopedia, listed in Jakarta, raising $1.1 billion at a valuation of about $28 billion. Some 300,000 investors participated, a record for the exchange.Step 6: Capital and Founders Recycle into the Ecosystem
As a startup ecosystem matures, its successes feed the next turn of the cycle in two ways. Exits send capital, founders, and experienced employees into the next generation of startups. And the incomes they create widen the pool of people who can participate.The most direct of those returns is capital. Across the cities in our research, a doubling of exits was followed by 27% more early-stage venture capital and 31% more late-stage capital the following year, and the effect was still present five years later. (See Exhibit 6.)

Founders and employees who have taken a company to a sale or public listing return with experience and relationships, and many of them are primed to share these advantages with the companies coming up behind them. SendGrid, an email delivery platform that went through Boulder, Colorado–based Techstars in 2009, became the first of its graduates to go public, in 2017, and Twilio acquired the company for about $3 billion two years later. The returns stayed close to home. Foundry Group, another company in the Denver-Boulder ecosystem, was among SendGrid’s early investors, and the former CEO who led SendGrid through its IPO is now a venture investor at Bessemer Venture Partners, backing other founders as they scale.The returns also reach people who never start a company. As incomes rise, more people can pursue higher education, develop new skills, and take the financial risks of entrepreneurship. Businesses, universities, and governments gain resources to invest in research and innovation. In São Paulo and Singapore, the lowest-paid workers shared in the gains as the cities matured. Real incomes among São Paulo’s bottom 40% rose by 9% from 2013 to 2024, outpacing the 7% gain for the top 10%, and poverty fell from 16.7% to 14.0%. In Singapore, incomes among the bottom 10% rose by 36% over the same period, against 32% for the top 10%, and inequality reached its lowest level on record in 2024. (See Exhibit 7.)

In each city, the growth of the entrepreneurial ecosystem contributed to those gains alongside other factors. Two of São Paulo’s largest startups built products for people who were unable to participate in the formal economy. Nubank’s fee-free bank account was designed for Brazilians without a bank account and had more than 100 million customers by 2024. Similarly, iFood, founded just outside the city in 2011, gave restaurants a sales channel and delivery workers an income. In Singapore, the growing ecosystem lifted incomes before taxes and transfers, and government programs, including the Workfare Income Supplement and the Progressive Wage Model, spread the gains to lower-paid workers.Enable the Cycle with Policy and Culture
Public policy can help build a startup ecosystem, but priorities need to adjust as the ecosystem develops. An ecosystem that has successfully invested in research and startup formation may gain little from adding more incubators if its young companies cannot win customers or secure expansion capital. The challenge for public officials is to recognize when an intervention has done its job and to move on, redirecting resources toward overcoming the next constraint on growth.Singapore illustrates how these priorities can evolve. A national technology plan committed S$2 billion to research in 1991. Its Industry 21 blueprint, introduced in 1999, sought to attract regional corporate headquarters and the commercial opportunities that they could offer local businesses. IP protections and favorable investment rules helped attract venture capital. More recently, the Global Innovation Alliance, launched in 2017, connected more than 700 startups and technology companies with overseas customers and investors by 2023. When the government announced its next research plan in 2025, committing S$37 billion through 2030, it cited the growth of the startup ecosystem as evidence that the earlier plans had worked.An ecosystem can have founders, investors, universities, and corporations on board and still get little from them if they rarely meet. Culture brings these stakeholders together so that experience, capital, and introductions move from the companies that have them to the companies that need them. The fast-maturing cities discussed in this section built that culture deliberately, and the resulting connections outlasted the effort that created them.Copenhagen’s TechBBQ, the founders’ gathering that we described in our earlier article, now pays for itself. By 2023, corporate foundations and partners including Google, Microsoft, and Danske Bank contributed €4 million, with public funds accounting for only a small fraction of its budget. The connections that the event was created to foster now help finance it. In Bangkok, informal gatherings begun in 2012 by entrepreneurs tired of traveling to Singapore for investors and conferences grew into Thailand Startup Week. In Barcelona, a 2011 meeting between the mayor and a successful local founder helped launch the city’s push to become a technology hub. Today, Barcelona has among the lowest rates of founder departure of the ecosystems we studied.The longer-term test of policy and culture is whether they make the ecosystem more and more capable of supporting its own growth. Public investment in research, education, and infrastructure remains important. But as businesses mature, commercial relationships deepen, and entrepreneurs reinvest their experience and capital, it is highly desirable for an increasing share of the connections needed for further growth to develop without fresh public intervention.

Cities have spent decades investing in entrepreneurship on the assumption that the ingredients were what mattered. However, the ecosystems that matured fastest show that the sequence of assembly matters at least as much and that getting the order right can cut the time required to develop a self-sustaining ecosystem roughly in half.That changes the calculation of what policy leaders can promise. Build IP and talent, and promising companies form. Bring in corporate customers, and those promising companies prove that they can sell. Capital then arrives at the scale needed for swift growth. From there the cycle runs on its own. More startups form, the best of them grow into large exits, and the capital and founders that those exits produce come back to fund and advise the companies following in their wake. Within a generation, the investment can become an economy that pays for its own next round of growth and raises incomes well beyond the startup scene.The fastest-maturing cities did not start with the same advantages, and few were well known when they began. What they shared was a willingness to build the next stage before the previous one had finished paying off. Other startup ecosystems can do the same. By following the EPC, they can build the engine of entrepreneurial capitalism.
